title: Geometric Signatures of Reasoning: A Spectral Perspective on Task Hardness
claim: Reasoning chains form hidden-state trajectories whose geometry reveals task hardness and predicts solution correctness early.
layout: Top pipeline strip over three panels A/B/C; left-to-right flow with histogram
description: A rounded top banner shows a left-to-right pipeline of icons and labels: Question, LLM (neural net), Trajectories (connected dots), a gray box reading 'Geometric Functionals (Effective Dimension)', and Hardness Prediction. Below are three rounded panels. Panel A, on the left, shows a sample math question in a blue box, the tokens of the chain-of-thought on a position axis, and a 3D hidden-state trajectory with h1 to hn and the formula γ=(H1..Hn)∈R^nd. Panel B shows a smooth blue EASY 3D curve next to a tangled orange HARD curve, with an overlapping blue/orange histogram of effective dimension d_ρ. Panel C shows a Hard Question going into a Trained LLM, then branching to a green CORRECT and a red INCORRECT trajectory. Solid segments are early and observed; faded dashed segments are later and unobserved. Blue, orange, green and red carry the meaning.
caption: Overview of our framework. A question is fed to an LLM whose chain-of-thought generation traces a discrete curve $\gamma = (h_1, \ldots, h_n) \in \R^d$ in hidden-state space. (A) Each generated token produces a hidden state, forming a trajectory whose geometry we analyze. (B) Empirically, hard problems exhibit higher-dimensional trajectories than easy ones at every tested model scale, providing a geometric measure of task hardness. (C) Whether a reasoning chain will reach a correct answer is partially detectable from geometric functionals of the early trajectory: kinematic features extracted from only the first $20%$ of generated tokens predict solution correctness with high AUC before generation is complete.
abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning enables large language models (LLMs) to solve complex problems by generating intermediate reasoning steps. While much attention has been paid to the length and content of these reasoning chains, far less is known about their internal geometry. We study the geometry of CoT trajectories in the hidden state space of transformer models, formalizing each reasoning chain as a discrete curve in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and characterizing it through spectral, positional, and kinematic geometric functionals. We introduce the effective dimension $d_Ï$ as a measure of trajectory complexity and empirically show that harder tasks exhibit greater effective dimension. Lastly, we explore how kinematic features of the trajectory, mean position, positional dispersion, initial and final hidden states, mean velocity, mean speed, and speed dispersion, can be used to predict solution correctness before generation is complete, and may inform future early-stopping strategies. Experimentally, on 86 mathematical reasoning problems from the MATH500 dataset and three Qwen2.5 model scales (0.5B, 1.5B, and 7B), $d_Ï$ achieves difficulty-prediction AUROC of $0.90$, $0.94$, and $0.96$, respectively. Seven kinematic and positional features predict correctness from only the first $20\%$ of generated tokens, with AUROC between $0.77$ and $0.88$ across scales. These correctness signatures transfer across held-out questions, establishing that the shape of a model's internal reasoning trajectory is a principled window into both task hardness and solution quality.
